stem: A 25-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has petechiae and bruising. Her platelet count is 30,000/mm³ with a normal hemoglobin and white count, and her smear shows a few large platelets. A bone marrow aspirate is examined under the microscope (see the picture).
oneliner: 25F + SLE + petechiae + platelets 30,000 + normal Hb and WBC + large platelets on smear + marrow aspirate → what does it show?
ask: Which bone marrow finding is expected?

whyNot.A: Would mean **underproduction**; large young platelets on the smear show the marrow is making plenty
whyNot.B: The picture of **myelofibrosis**; her hemoglobin and white count are normal
whyNot.C: **Aplastic anemia** causes pancytopenia; here only platelets are low
whyNot.D: **Acute leukemia** gives pancytopenia and blasts on the smear

why: In **immune thrombocytopenia**, **autoantibodies coat platelets** and splenic macrophages destroy them. The marrow responds with **more megakaryocytes**, and the peripheral smear shows **large young platelets**. Other cell lines are normal.

idea.rule: Peripheral platelet destruction = megakaryocytes increased in the marrow; underproduction = decreased.
also: TTP and DIC also show increased megakaryocytes
Aplastic anemia: empty fatty marrow with pancytopenia
Myelofibrosis: dry tap with teardrop cells
SLE is a recognized cause of secondary ITP

stem: A 4-year-old boy is pale and mildly jaundiced. Hemoglobin is low, MCHC is raised, reticulocytes are high and indirect bilirubin is elevated. The spleen tip is palpable, and his father had a splenectomy in youth. His peripheral smear is shown (see the picture).
oneliner: 4M + pallor + jaundice + high MCHC + reticulocytosis + palpable spleen + father splenectomized → which red cell finding?
ask: Which red cell finding is expected on the smear?

options.A: Cells with a dark central spot and a pale ring around it
options.B: Fragmented helmet-shaped cells with sharp edges
options.C: Small round dense cells with no central pallor, plus bluish cells
options.D: Cells with a bitten-out edge and purple inclusions on supravital stain
options.E: Large oval red cells with hypersegmented neutrophils nearby

whyNot.A: **Target cells** suit thalassemia, liver disease or HbC, with a low MCHC, not a high one
whyNot.B: **Schistocytes** mean mechanical destruction (DIC, TTP, valve), not a familial anemia with a high MCHC
whyNot.D: **Bite cells and Heinz bodies** suggest G6PD deficiency, which is X-linked and cannot pass from father to son
whyNot.E: **Macro-ovalocytes** mean B12 or folate lack with a poor marrow response; his reticulocytes are high

why: Loss of membrane (ankyrin or spectrin defect) leaves **small dense spheres with no central pallor**, hence the **high MCHC**. The spleen removes them, so there are **reticulocytosis, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and splenomegaly**.

idea.rule: Round dense red cells without pallor mean membrane has been lost, either inherited or antibody-coated.
also: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia: spherocytes with a positive direct Coombs test
Hereditary spherocytosis: osmotic fragility and a negative Coombs test
Spherocytes are removed by splenic macrophages (extravascular hemolysis)

stem: A 65-year-old man has two months of back pain and fatigue. Serum calcium is high, creatinine is rising, and hemoglobin is low with normal cell size. X-ray shows punched-out lesions in the iliac bone, and serum protein electrophoresis shows a large IgG spike. His bone marrow aspirate is shown (see the picture).
oneliner: 65M + back pain + lytic iliac lesions + high calcium + rising creatinine + anemia + IgG spike → which marrow finding?
ask: Which bone marrow finding is expected?

options.A: Sheets of large primitive cells with needle-shaped cytoplasmic rods
options.B: Small mature lymphocytes with many crushed smudged nuclei
options.C: Large cells with grooved nuclei mixed with eosinophils
options.D: Glandular clusters of cells with mucin vacuoles
options.E: Sheets of cells with off-center nuclei and a perinuclear clear zone

whyNot.A: **Myeloblasts with Auer rods** are acute myeloid leukemia, with cytopenias and no monoclonal spike
whyNot.B: **Small mature lymphocytes and smudge cells** are CLL; no lytic bone lesions or hypercalcemia
whyNot.C: **Grooved nuclei with eosinophils** are Langerhans cells (CD1a, Birbeck granules), a histiocytosis without an IgG spike
whyNot.D: **Metastatic carcinoma** can cause lytic lesions and hypercalcemia, but a monoclonal IgG spike and plasma-cell morphology are absent

answer: Marrow replaced by sheets of plasma cells
why: A malignant **plasma-cell clone** fills the marrow, makes **monoclonal IgG** and drives osteoclasts to cause **lytic lesions and hypercalcemia**. Light chains injure the kidney, and **eccentric nuclei, clock-face chromatin and a perinuclear hof** are the plasma-cell look.

idea.rule: Plasma cells have eccentric nuclei, clock-face chromatin and a perinuclear clearing (Golgi).
also: Rouleaux of red cells on the blood smear
Russell bodies (cytoplasmic immunoglobulin) and Dutcher bodies (nuclear)
Bence Jones protein and cast nephropathy in the kidney

stem: A 63-year-old man has two months of left upper abdominal fullness, weight loss and fatigue. He is pale with a spleen reaching the pelvic brim, and uric acid is high. A marrow aspiration attempt yields no fluid. A blood smear and biopsy are sent.
oneliner: 63M + LUQ fullness + weight loss + massive splenomegaly + anemia + high uric acid + dry tap → which smear and biopsy findings?
ask: Which pair of findings is expected?

options.A: Spherocytes with polychromatic cells; hypocellular marrow
options.B: Teardrop cells and nucleated red cells with early granulocytes; fibrotic marrow
options.C: Fragmented red cells with low platelets; hypercellular marrow with many megakaryocytes
options.D: Smudged mature lymphocytes; marrow packed with small lymphocytes
options.E: Blasts with needle-shaped rods; marrow full of blasts

whyNot.A: **Spherocytes** mean membrane-loss hemolysis; a **dry tap** points to a fibrotic, not hypocellular, marrow
whyNot.C: **Schistocytes with low platelets** mean microangiopathy; there is no fibrosis or dry tap
whyNot.D: **Smudge cells** are CLL, where the marrow is **full of small lymphocytes**, not scarred
whyNot.E: **Myeloblasts with Auer rods** are acute leukemia; a **dry tap with a spleen reaching the pelvis** favors fibrosis

answer: Leukoerythroblastic smear with teardrop cells; marrow replaced by reticulin fibrosis
why: Marrow **fibrosis** crowds blood cells out, causing a **dry tap**, and blood-forming cells move to the spleen (**extramedullary hematopoiesis**), which gives **massive splenomegaly**. Squeezing through fibrotic marrow and spleen makes **teardrop cells**, and immature cells spill out as a **leukoerythroblastic** picture.

idea.rule: Dry tap + teardrop cells + massive spleen = marrow fibrosis.
also: JAK2 V617F is present in about half of cases
Fibrosis is driven by megakaryocyte release of PDGF and TGF-beta
Can follow polycythemia vera or essential thrombocythemia

stem: A 3-year-old boy has had two days of a bulging, painful right eye with no fever or injury. MRI shows a mass within the muscles that move the eye, pushing the globe forward. A biopsy is taken.
oneliner: 3M + 2 days of painful proptosis + mass in extraocular muscles + no trauma → which biopsy feature?
ask: Which biopsy feature identifies this tumor?

options.A: Ring-shaped rosettes with a hollow center and photoreceptor features
options.B: Rosettes around a central tangle of fibrils
options.C: Sheets of lymphoid cells with pale macrophages, giving a starry-sky look
options.D: Malignant cells with cross-banded cytoplasm that stain for desmin

whyNot.A: **Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes** mean retinoblastoma, which is inside the globe (leukocoria), not in the muscles
whyNot.B: **Homer Wright rosettes** mean neuroblastoma or medulloblastoma, not a muscle mass
whyNot.C: **Starry-sky** pattern is Burkitt lymphoma, a jaw or abdominal mass with no muscle differentiation
whyNot.E: **Psammoma bodies** belong to meningioma, papillary thyroid and serous ovarian tumors, not a muscle mass in a toddler

why: This is **embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma**, the commonest soft-tissue sarcoma in children, arising from **primitive skeletal-muscle cells**. Some malignant cells show **cross-striations** and stain for **desmin and myogenin**.

idea.rule: A skeletal-muscle tumor shows rhabdomyoblasts with cross-striations and desmin.
also: Sarcoma botryoides: grape-like vaginal mass in a girl, desmin positive
Also arises in the head and neck, bladder and paratesticular region
Alveolar subtype has t(2;13) PAX3-FOXO1

stem: A 70-year-old man has a lymphocyte count of 60,000/mm3 found on a routine blood test. He feels well, but has several painless, rubbery neck and axillary nodes. Flow cytometry shows B cells expressing CD5 and CD23.
oneliner: 70M + routine count with 60,000 lymphocytes + painless nodes + CD5/CD23 B cells → which smear finding?

options.A: Fused needle-shaped granules in myeloid precursors
options.B: Large lymphoid cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and nucleoli
options.D: Neutrophils with coarse granules and blue cytoplasmic inclusions
options.E: Many small mature lymphocytes with crushed, smeared nuclei

whyNot.A: **Auer rods** mean acute myeloid leukemia, with blasts and cytopenias
whyNot.B: **Lymphoblasts** mean an acute leukemia with marrow failure, which would not leave a 70-year-old feeling well
whyNot.C: **Hairy projections** are hairy cell leukemia, which is CD5 negative and CD103 positive; these cells are CD5+ CD23+
whyNot.D: **Toxic granulation and Dohle bodies** are neutrophil changes from infection, not lymphocytosis

answer: Mature small lymphocytes with smudge cells
why: CD5 and CD23 on mature B cells means **chronic lymphocytic leukemia**. The fragile small lymphocytes are **crushed during smearing** and appear as **smudge cells** among many mature-looking lymphocytes.

idea.rule: CD5+ CD23+ B-cell lymphocytosis in an older adult gives small lymphocytes and smudge cells.
also: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia can complicate CLL
Hypogammaglobulinemia causes recurrent infections
Richter transformation to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

stem: A 28-year-old man with HIV, not on treatment and with a CD4 count of 90/mm3, has developed multiple purple-brown, nonpainful, nonulcerated skin nodules over his legs. There is no fever or drainage. A punch biopsy is taken.
oneliner: 28M + untreated HIV + CD4 90 + purple nonulcerated nodules → which biopsy finding?

options.B: Plump spindle cells forming slit-like spaces containing red cells
options.D: Neutrophil-rich capillary proliferation with clumps of small bacilli
options.E: Large cells with glassy intranuclear inclusions and multinucleation

whyNot.A: **Intracellular yeast** suggests histoplasmosis, which gives fever and visceral disease rather than painless purple nodules
whyNot.C: **Acid-fast bacilli** suggest mycobacterial infection, which causes ulcers or nodules with caseation
whyNot.D: **Bacillary angiomatosis** (Bartonella) has neutrophils and bacilli, with red friable lesions and fever; he is afebrile
whyNot.E: **Herpes inclusions** give painful vesicles and ulcers, not firm purple nodules

answer: Spindle cells lining slit-like vascular spaces
why: Low CD4 allows **HHV-8** to drive endothelial-derived **spindle cell** growth, forming **slit-like vascular spaces filled with red cells**, which look purple. This is **Kaposi sarcoma**, an AIDS-defining cancer.

idea.rule: Purple-brown nodules in HIV with spindle cells and slits mean Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8).
also: Bacillary angiomatosis (Bartonella) is the main mimic, with neutrophils and bacilli
Immune reconstitution with antiretrovirals can shrink lesions
HHV-8 also causes primary effusion lymphoma and Castleman disease

stem: A 55-year-old man has had a painless, rubbery cervical lymph node for months that has shrunk and grown again. He feels well. Flow cytometry of the excised node shows B cells that are CD10 positive with kappa light chains only. Node architecture is examined.
oneliner: 55M + painless node waxing and waning + CD10+ B cells + kappa only → which node architecture?
ask: Which lymph node architecture is expected?

options.A: Diffuse sheets of large cells with open chromatin
options.B: Sheets of medium cells studded with debris-laden macrophages
options.C: Scattered large binucleate cells in a mixed inflammatory background
options.D: Crowded back-to-back follicles replacing the normal architecture
options.E: Follicles with a polarized germinal center and tingible-body macrophages

whyNot.A: **Diffuse large B cell lymphoma** grows fast and is aggressive; this node waxes and wanes
whyNot.B: **Burkitt lymphoma** is rapidly growing with a very high mitotic rate, not an indolent course
whyNot.C: **Reed-Sternberg cells** are Hodgkin lymphoma (CD15, CD30), not a clonal CD10 kappa B-cell population
whyNot.E: **Reactive follicles** are polyclonal with both kappa and lambda cells and keep normal architecture

answer: Back-to-back neoplastic follicles that efface the node
why: **t(14;18)** puts **BCL2** next to the IgH locus, so B cells resist apoptosis and form **monoclonal, crowded follicles** replacing the node. **CD10 and light-chain restriction** mark the clonal B cells, and the course is **indolent**.

idea.rule: Follicles that are crowded, monotonous and monoclonal (BCL2+) mean follicular lymphoma.
also: Reactive follicles are polarized, polyclonal and BCL2 negative
t(14;18) leads to BCL2 overexpression
Can transform to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

stem: A 65-year-old man dies of renal failure after a year of weakness, weight loss and foamy urine. Urine contained Bence Jones protein. At autopsy his kidneys are enlarged and pale, and the glomeruli are expanded by acellular pink material. Renal sections are stained.
oneliner: 65M + renal failure + Bence Jones protein + foamy urine + enlarged kidneys with acellular glomerular material → which stain result?
ask: Which stain result confirms the nature of the glomerular material?

options.A: Apple-green birefringence with Congo red under polarized light
options.B: Pink globules on PAS stain that resist diastase
options.C: Blue granules in macrophages on Prussian blue stain
options.D: Basement membrane spikes on silver stain
options.E: Fractured tubular casts ringed by giant cells on H&E

whyNot.B: **PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules** are alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in the liver
whyNot.C: **Prussian blue** granules mean hemosiderin iron, as in hemochromatosis
whyNot.D: **Spikes** on silver stain mean membranous nephropathy, with no Bence Jones protein or acellular glomerular material
whyNot.E: **Cast nephropathy** fits Bence Jones protein but sits in tubules, not glomeruli, and does not cause foamy urine

why: Light chains from a plasma cell clone form **AL amyloid**, **beta-pleated sheets** deposited outside cells, enlarging the kidney and causing **nephrotic-range proteinuria**. **Congo red** stains the deposits, which show **apple-green birefringence** under polarized light.

idea.rule: Amyloid = Congo red with apple-green birefringence in polarized light.
also: AL amyloid from light chains in plasma cell dyscrasias
AA amyloid from serum amyloid A in chronic inflammation
Transthyretin amyloid in the aging heart

stem: A 3-month-old girl is brought in with blue lips and gray skin. She has been fed formula mixed with water from a private well. Pulse oximetry reads 85%, which does not improve with oxygen, but arterial PO2 is normal. A blood sample is drawn.
oneliner: 3-month F + cyanosis + well-water formula + SpO2 85% not corrected by oxygen + normal arterial PO2 → what does the blood look like?
ask: What is the appearance of the drawn blood?

options.A: Cherry red, staying red in air
options.C: Dark red turning bright red when shaken in air
options.D: Milky plasma with a creamy top layer
options.E: Chocolate-brown that stays brown in air

whyNot.A: **Cherry-red** blood is carboxyhemoglobin from carbon monoxide; her exposure is nitrate-rich well water
whyNot.B: **Bright red** blood implies well-oxygenated hemoglobin; here saturation is low
whyNot.C: **Dark venous blood** reddens in air because normal hemoglobin binds oxygen; this blood does not
whyNot.D: **Lipemic plasma** comes from hypertriglyceridemia and would not cause cyanosis

answer: Chocolate-brown blood that does not redden in air
why: Nitrates in well water are converted to nitrites, which oxidize iron to **Fe3+ (methemoglobin)**. Fe3+ hemoglobin **cannot carry oxygen**, causing **cyanosis with normal PO2** and **chocolate-brown blood** unaffected by oxygen.

idea.rule: Cyanosis that oxygen does not fix, with normal PO2 and brown blood, means methemoglobin (Fe3+).
also: Dapsone, benzocaine and nitrites are triggers
Treat with methylene blue (IV), which reduces Fe3+ to Fe2+
Pulse oximetry is stuck near 85%

stem: A 63-year-old man from southern China has had a blocked right ear and blood-streaked nasal discharge for three months. He has a hard, fixed node high in the posterior neck. An excised node is stained.
oneliner: 63M + southern Chinese + bloody nasal discharge + blocked ear + upper posterior neck node → which stain result?
ask: Which immunostain result identifies the tumor cells?

whyNot.A: **CD19/CD20** mark a B-cell lymphoma; southern Chinese ancestry with a nasal bleed and blocked ear points to an epithelial nasopharyngeal primary
whyNot.C: **CD15 and CD30** mark Reed-Sternberg cells of Hodgkin lymphoma, which is also EBV-linked but is not keratin positive
whyNot.D: **CD1a and S-100** mark Langerhans cells in histiocytosis, a bone and skin disease, not a nasopharyngeal mass
whyNot.E: **Desmin and myogenin** mark muscle tumors such as rhabdomyosarcoma, a childhood tumor, not a 63-year-old's nasal cancer

why: A nasopharyngeal primary spreads to **upper posterior cervical nodes**. The tumor cells are **epithelial (keratin positive)** and **EBV positive**, which separates **nasopharyngeal carcinoma** from an EBV-linked lymphoma.

idea.rule: EBV-positive epithelial (keratin) cells in a neck node mean nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
also: Common in southern China and North Africa
Anti-EBV VCA IgA is elevated
Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma and CNS lymphoma in HIV are other EBV tumors

stem: A 60-year-old man has had weight loss, iron deficiency anemia and signs of large-bowel obstruction. A segment of colon is resected and examined by the pathologist, who must decide whether the mass is cancer.
oneliner: 60M + weight loss + iron deficiency + large-bowel obstruction + resected colon mass → which feature best supports malignancy?
ask: Which feature most strongly supports malignancy?

options.D: Tumor growing into the muscular wall

whyNot.A: **Narrowing** also occurs in benign strictures from Crohn disease, ischemia or diverticulitis
whyNot.B: **Ulcers** occur in colitis and ischemia as well, so they do not prove cancer
whyNot.C: **Fibrosis** is the result of chronic injury and healing, as in Crohn or radiation damage
whyNot.E: A **sharp border** can be seen with adenomas and benign lesions, so it does not show invasion

answer: Invasion through the submucosa into the muscular wall
why: Cancer is defined by **invasion** across the basement membrane and beyond the muscularis mucosae, here into **submucosa and muscularis propria**. **Narrowing, ulceration, fibrosis and a sharp edge** appear in benign disease too.

idea.rule: Malignancy is proven by invasion (and metastasis), not by how a lesion looks.
also: Carcinoma in situ stays above the basement membrane
Invasion into the submucosa is what lets a colon polyp metastasize
Metastasis is the other absolute sign of malignancy

stem: A 26-year-old woman has a metastatic tumor whose tissue of origin cannot be identified on light microscopy. Immunostaining of the biopsy is strongly positive for desmin.
oneliner: 26F + metastatic tumor, origin unclear on microscopy + desmin-positive → which cell features define it?
ask: Which microscopic features best define a tumor like this?

options.A: Uniform cells with a low nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio
options.B: Cells that closely resemble their tissue of origin
options.C: Pleomorphic nuclei, high N:C ratio, atypical mitoses
options.D: More cells of normal type with normal architecture
options.E: One mature cell type replaced by another type

whyNot.A: Uniform cells with a low N:C ratio fit a **benign or well-differentiated** lesion; this tumor's **origin cannot be seen** on microscopy
whyNot.B: That is **good differentiation**; here the origin is invisible on microscopy and needed an **immunostain (desmin)**
whyNot.D: That is **hyperplasia**, a non-neoplastic change, not a **metastatic** tumor
whyNot.E: That is **metaplasia**, an adaptation of mature cells, not a **metastatic** tumor of unclear origin

answer: Anaplasia: pleomorphic, hyperchromatic nuclei, high N:C ratio, prominent nucleoli, atypical mitoses
why: **Anaplasia** means loss of differentiation, so the cells look **nothing like their tissue of origin** and show **nuclear pleomorphism, a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, prominent nucleoli and atypical mitoses**. **Immunostains** such as **desmin** (muscle) then reveal the lineage, here a muscle-derived tumor.

idea.rule: Anaplasia = the cells have lost all resemblance to their parent tissue.
also: Marked nuclear pleomorphism with tumor giant cells
Abnormal (e.g. tripolar) mitotic figures
Loss of polarity: cells grow in disorganized sheets
The less differentiated a tumor, the higher its grade

stem: An 80-year-old man who lives alone and eats mostly tea and toast has easy bruising and slow healing of a minor cut. Examination of his mouth and skin is performed. Prothrombin time and platelet count are normal.
oneliner: 80M + lives alone, tea and toast diet + easy bruising + poor wound healing + normal PT and platelets → which mouth and skin findings?
ask: Which findings are most likely on examination?

options.A: Bleeding gums, perifollicular bleeds, corkscrew hairs
options.B: Smooth red tongue with cracks at the mouth corners
options.D: Scaly pigmented rash on sun-exposed skin
options.E: Scattered petechiae from a low platelet count

whyNot.B: Glossitis and angular cheilitis suggest **B-vitamin or iron deficiency**; they do not explain **easy bruising and slow wound healing**
whyNot.C: Koilonychia is a sign of **iron deficiency**; it does not explain **bruising with poor wound healing**
whyNot.D: **Pellagra** (niacin deficiency) causes this; it does not cause **bruising with poor wound healing**
whyNot.E: His **platelet count is normal**, so thrombocytopenic bleeding is excluded

answer: Scurvy: swollen bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew hairs
why: A diet **without fruit or vegetables** causes **vitamin C deficiency**. Without vitamin C, **proline and lysine cannot be hydroxylated**, so collagen is weak: **gums bleed, perifollicular hemorrhages and corkscrew hairs** appear and wounds heal poorly, with **normal PT and platelets**.

idea.rule: Vitamin C deficiency = weak collagen: bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhage, corkscrew hairs, poor healing.
also: Subperiosteal hemorrhage with bone pain in children
Bleeding into joints (hemarthrosis)
Loosened teeth and reopening of old scars
Normal PT and platelet count despite the bleeding
